My view is thus summed up by an able court which made no finding 
that there had actually been sharp practice. Rather the appellant seems 
to have known precisely where she stood. 
There are many aspects of public policy here involved. What is a 
luxury to some may seem an outright necessity to others. Is public 
oversight to be required of the expenditures of relief funds? A washing 
machine, e.g., in the hands of a relief client might become a fruitful source 
of income. Many relief clients may well need credit, and certain business 
establishments will take long chances on the sale of items, expecting 
their pricing policies will afford a degree of protection commensurate 
with the ris.{. Perhaps a remedy when necessary will be found within the 
provisions of the "Loan Shark" law, D.C.Code Sections 26-601 et seq. 
(1961). 
I mention 
such matters 
only to emphasize the desirability of a 
cautious approach to any such problem, particularly since the law for so 
long has allowed parties such great latitude in making their own 
contracts. I dare say there must annually be thousands upon thousands 
of installment 
credit transactions 
in this jurisdiction, and one can only 
speculate as to the effect the decision in these cases will have. 10 
I join the District of Columbia Court of Appeals in its disposition of 
the issues. 
NOTES 
(1) Questions. What exactly did the court hold? What should the trial 
court do on remand? What are dissenting Judge Danaher's concerns about 
the majority's decision? 
What is offensive about the allocation of payment provision? It may help 
to know that another way to apportion a payment is in relation to the 
original debt for each item. If the store had applied Mrs. Williams's 
payments that way, she would evidently have paid in full for about a dozen 
of the 16 items she bought from the store. Could the store have been 
compelled to reallocate her payments in that manner, as a plausible reading 
of the contract? 
What is offensive about the cross-collateral or "dragnet" clause? Under 
this provision the seller is entitled to repossess one item for the buyer's 
failure to pay for another. If the repossessed items are resold for less than 
~he buyer's indebtedness, the seller is generally entitled to a deficiency 
Judgment for the difference. If they are resold for more than is due, the seller
